description: CLEARANCE GAP Library v1.9.4 — deterministic engine complete. 25 gaps, 4 vertical layers, 26 signals. V1.9.4 renames severity_logic → exposure_logic and likelihood_logic → recurrence_logic across all 25 gaps, aligning field names with CLEARANCE's identity as a governance exposure calculator, not a risk scoring model. Engine remains fully deterministic end-to-end: signal → gap → exposure → priority.
gap_definition: A gap = a single, observable control failure, with clear evidence signals and an implied remediation path

severity_scale.CRITICAL: Compound or acute failure — immediate regulatory exposure, multiple simultaneous obligations breached
severity_scale.HIGH: Direct regulatory or legal enforcement exposure — named obligation unmet, enforcement trigger present
severity_scale.MEDIUM: Process or documentation gap — real risk but no immediate single enforcement trigger

domain_architecture.description: Three-layer model separating universal controls from vertical-specific gaps

layer_1_core.label: Core
layer_1_core.description: Structural governance gaps applicable to every agentic AI deployment regardless of sector

layer_2_hr.label: HR Vertical
layer_2_hr.description: Gaps specific to AI use across the employee lifecycle — hiring, monitoring, performance, discipline

layer_3_legal.label: Legal Vertical
layer_3_legal.description: Gaps specific to AI use in legal service delivery — drafting, research, client obligations

layer_4_finserv.label: Financial Services Control Layer (FCA-aligned)
layer_4_finserv.description: Gaps specific to AI use in FCA-regulated financial services — suitability, SM&CR accountability, audit trail, Consumer Duty outcome monitoring, and algorithmic fairness

pipeline_definition.description: End-to-end execution flow from intake to report

steps.name: Input
steps.description: Completed intake form received and verified call conducted
outputs: Structured intake object with controls, signals and incident data

steps.name: Signal detection
steps.description: Intake answers mapped to signal boolean values. Controls (rule_enforcement, audit_trail, logging) resolved to no_rule_enforcement, no_audit_trail, no_logging signals first. All signals resolved before gap engine runs.
outputs: Signal map: {signal_id: true|false} for all 26 signals
steps.logic: See signals_definition for derivation rules per signal

steps.name: Gap activation
steps.description: Signal map evaluated against each gap's expr logic
outputs: Activated gap list with severity and domain context
steps.logic: Evaluate expr AST for each gap; include gap if expr resolves to true

steps.name: Scoring
steps.description: Aggregate risk across activated gaps by domain layer
outputs: Risk score per gap, aggregate posture rating (LOW/MODERATE/HIGH/CRITICAL)
steps.logic: Use risk_score.priority per gap; overall = highest priority across activated gaps

steps.name: Report generation
steps.description: Produce prioritised client report from activated gaps
steps.logic: Use sector_risk narrative for client-facing text; sort by priority ascending

gaps.title: No decision boundary enforcement
gaps.description: There is no rule between what this AI system decides and what it does. You have a system that produces an output and that output becomes an action — nothing checks whether it should. When something goes wrong, you cannot show what governed the decision. Because nothing did.
evidence_signals: Ask what rules govern this AI system. The answer is: there are none documented
The system produces an output and that output becomes an action — with nothing in between
No version-controlled policy exists defining what this system is and is not permitted to decide
Agent errors reach production with no interception point

risk.regulatory: Without a rule enforcement layer, you cannot show a regulator that this system was governed. That matters under UK GDPR, the FCA's operational standards and the SRA Code, depending on your sector. The absence of rules is not a gap to be filled — it is the finding.
risk.operational: When this system makes a mistake, it goes straight through to the client, the patient, or the employee. There is no catch. The first sign something is wrong is when someone affected tells you.
risk.reputational: If something goes wrong and you are asked what governance existed — the answer is none. That is a very difficult position to be in front of a board, an insurer or a regulator.

remediation: Introduce a step between this system's output and the action it takes. Even a simple documented ruleset — defining what the system is and is not allowed to decide — is a material improvement on nothing.
Write down the rules. What decisions is this system allowed to make? What should it escalate? Version-control the document so you can show it has been maintained.
Assign someone to own the ruleset. Their name, their role, their sign-off on any change. That is the minimum that makes this defensible.

dpia_mapping.processing_description: Automated decision-making by AI agent with no intermediate rule evaluation
dpia_mapping.risk: High — automated decisions execute without governance control, creating uncontrolled processing with legal or significant effects on individuals
dpia_mapping.mitigation: Implement rule enforcement layer; document decision logic; introduce human override mechanism
dpia_mapping.residual_risk: Medium — after rule enforcement layer implemented, residual risk from rule configuration errors; requires version control and change management

gaps.pain_line: This becomes visible after an incident — when someone asks what governance existed, and the honest answer is: none.
gaps.severity_plain: Creates direct regulatory exposure. Without a rule enforcement layer, the organisation cannot demonstrate to a regulator, insurer or court that this AI system was governed. That position is very difficult to defend.
gaps.what_happens_next: Introduce a rule evaluation layer between this system's output and the action it takes. Even a minimal documented ruleset is a material improvement on none. These issues can be identified and prioritised through a focused review of your AI decision flows.

exposure_logic.note: High-impact decisions without override — boundary failure is immediately consequential

recurrence_logic.note: Known incidents confirm gap is not hypothetical
No ruleset at all — gap is structural, not partial

gaps.title: Provenance weakness
gaps.description: You are acting on data you cannot fully account for. Some of it comes from outside the organisation. None of it is validated before it reaches the system. If the data is wrong, the decision is wrong — and you cannot trace either back to a source.
evidence_signals: Ask where the data feeding this system comes from. The full answer is not available
External data sources are ingested with no validation step before they reach the system
No data source register exists documenting origin, update frequency and owner for each input
Input data quality is assumed, not verified

risk.regulatory: UK GDPR requires personal data to be accurate. If this system is making decisions about people based on unverified data, that is a breach of the accuracy principle — and it is difficult to defend if someone challenges a decision.
risk.operational: When a decision turns out to be based on bad data, you cannot reconstruct what happened. You do not know what the system received, so you cannot explain what it did. Root cause analysis becomes guesswork.
risk.reputational: Standard AI liability policies are starting to require documented input validation. Without it, an insurer has grounds to query a claim. That is worth knowing before something goes wrong.

remediation: List every data source feeding this system. Where does it come from? Who owns it? When was it last updated? Write that down. That list is your starting point.
Add a basic validation check before data reaches the system. At a minimum, flag inputs that fall outside expected ranges or schemas before they inform a decision.
Assign an owner to each data source. One person who is responsible for its accuracy and who gets notified when something looks wrong.

dpia_mapping.processing_description: AI processing of unverified or untraced external data in automated decision-making
dpia_mapping.risk: Medium — decisions based on inaccurate or unverified data produces unfair or incorrect outcomes affecting individuals
dpia_mapping.mitigation: Data source register; input validation layer; owner assignment per source; DPIA covering data quality controls
dpia_mapping.residual_risk: Low-medium — after validation implemented, residual risk from data drift between validation runs; requires monitoring cadence

gaps.pain_line: This becomes visible after an incident — when someone asks what data the system was acting on, and the honest answer is: we are not sure.
gaps.severity_plain: Creates exposure under UK GDPR Article 5(1)(d). Decisions based on unverified inputs cannot be reconstructed if challenged. That is difficult to defend in any regulatory investigation.
gaps.what_happens_next: Create a register of every data source feeding this system. Assign an owner and a validation status to each. These issues can be identified and prioritised through a focused review of your AI data inputs.

exposure_logic.note: Unvalidated external data elevates severity — corrupted inputs produce corrupted decisions

recurrence_logic.note: Known incidents involving data quality confirm provenance weakness is active
External data present — provenance risk is live

gaps.title: Audit void
gaps.description: If someone asks what this system decided on a specific date, you cannot tell them. There is no sealed record of what the system decided or why. The logs that do exist can be changed. When something goes wrong, you are piecing together what happened — not looking it up.
evidence_signals: Ask for the record of a specific decision made last month. It cannot be produced
Decision logs exist but are not write-once — they can be altered after the fact
No retention policy governs how long decision records are kept
Root cause analysis after an incident relies on reconstruction, not retrieval

risk.regulatory: UK GDPR gives individuals the right to contest automated decisions. That right requires a record to exist. Without one, you cannot respond. FCA and SRA requirements on record-keeping apply equally. Not having a record is itself a breach — separate from whatever the decision was.
risk.operational: When something goes wrong, you cannot find out what the system did, when it did it, or what it was acting on. You cannot investigate. You cannot learn from it. Every incident becomes more damaging because you have no account of what happened.
risk.reputational: Being unable to produce a decision record when a regulator, insurer or board asks for one is a significant red flag — independent of whether the underlying decision was right. It signals that the system has been running without oversight.

remediation: Start logging every decision today. For each one: the date, what went in, what came out, what rule was applied. Store it in a way that cannot be edited after the fact.
Move from basic logging to a proper evidence record. Input received, rule applied, decision made, timestamp. Sealed. Immutable. That is what you show a regulator.
Decide how long you keep records. Write that down. Align it to whatever your sector requires.

dpia_mapping.processing_description: Automated decision-making by AI agent with no sealed contemporaneous record of decisions
dpia_mapping.risk: High — inability to demonstrate lawfulness of processing; inability to respond to data subject rights requests; inability to evidence regulatory compliance
dpia_mapping.mitigation: Implement sealed write-once audit trail; define retention policy; enable decision retrieval on request
dpia_mapping.residual_risk: Low — after sealed audit trail implemented, residual risk from storage failure; requires backup and integrity verification

gaps.pain_line: This becomes visible after a complaint or challenge — when someone asks for the decision record, and you cannot produce one.
gaps.severity_plain: Creates direct exposure under UK GDPR Article 22C, FCA Principle 3 and SRA Code Rule 2.2 depending on sector. Absence of a sealed audit trail is itself a breach — independent of whether any underlying decision was wrong.
gaps.what_happens_next: Start logging every decision this system makes today — date, input, output, rule applied — in a write-once store. This is the foundation. Every other governance control depends on it existing. These issues can be identified and prioritised through a focused review of your AI decision records.

exposure_logic.note: Incidents occurred with no audit record — unknown harm cannot be quantified or defended
No sealed record — every decision made is individually indefensible

recurrence_logic.note: Known gap with no corrective action — breach is ongoing and accumulating
Zero logging — gap is complete, not partial

gaps.title: Accountability gap
gaps.description: You have a named person who would carry responsibility if this system caused harm. But ask them to show what oversight they exercised last month — and there is nothing to show. The title exists. The mechanism does not. Being named as accountable without a way to evidence you were in control is not protection. It is personal liability.
evidence_signals: The person accountable for this AI system cannot point to a single oversight action they took in the last 90 days
No override mechanism exists — the accountable individual cannot intervene before a decision executes
No oversight log exists showing when the system was reviewed, challenged or corrected
Escalation conditions are not defined — every decision runs automatically regardless of risk

risk.regulatory: Every sector has a requirement for a named individual to own AI-influenced outcomes. UK GDPR, SM&CR, DCB0160, SRA — they all name the person, not the team. If that person cannot show they exercised oversight, they cannot discharge the obligation. Having the title without the record does not help.
risk.operational: When a decision causes harm, the accountable individual will be asked what they did to stay in control. If the answer is nothing on record, that is a personal liability — not just an organisational one.
risk.reputational: A board, an insurer or a regulator asking for evidence of oversight expects a record, not a job description. The absence of an oversight log is read as evidence that oversight was not exercised.

remediation: This week: have the accountable individual start keeping a log. Date, what was reviewed, what was decided. A simple document is enough. The record is what matters.
Define the conditions under which a decision gets escalated to that person before it runs. Write them down. Make sure the system or the team knows what those conditions are.
Make sure the accountable individual has a real mechanism to stop or change a decision — not just in theory, but in practice. If they cannot intervene, they cannot be meaningfully accountable.

dpia_mapping.processing_description: Automated decision-making with legal or significant effects on individuals and no named human accountable for oversight
dpia_mapping.risk: High — individuals affected by AI decisions have no named human to appeal to; organisation has no mechanism to evidence governance was exercised
dpia_mapping.mitigation: Designate named accountable individual; implement override mechanism; establish oversight log; define escalation conditions
dpia_mapping.residual_risk: Low-medium — after accountability structure implemented, residual risk from accountable individual changing roles; requires succession plan and handover documentation

gaps.pain_line: This becomes visible after a harmful decision — when the accountable individual is asked what oversight they exercised, and there is nothing to show.
gaps.severity_plain: Creates personal liability exposure for a named individual. Without an oversight record, the person formally accountable cannot demonstrate they were in control. That is very difficult to defend at board level, in an investigation, or in court.
gaps.what_happens_next: Have the accountable individual start an oversight log this week — date, decision reviewed, action taken or confirmed. Even a simple log converts a job title into a defensible position. These issues can be identified and prioritised through a focused review of your AI accountability structure.

exposure_logic.note: High-impact decisions, no named owner, no override — accountability is completely absent

recurrence_logic.note: Incidents with no accountable individual — pattern of ungoverned operation confirmed

gaps.title: Remediation path absent
gaps.description: You have multiple governance gaps and no plan to close any of them. You are aware of the problems. Nothing has been done. Every new AI system you deploy in this state adds to the risk. Regulators do not treat this as an oversight. They treat it as a choice.
evidence_signals: Ask for the AI governance roadmap. It does not exist — not even a one-page outline with milestones
An incident or near-miss has occurred and no corrective action was documented or taken
Multiple governance gaps are present simultaneously with no remediation plan
New AI systems are being deployed without governance review

risk.regulatory: A pattern of identified gaps with no corrective action is the worst thing to show a regulator. The ICO, FCA, SRA and CQC all treat the absence of a plan as evidence of wilful non-compliance. It is harder to defend than any individual gap.
risk.operational: Without a plan, the gap between how quickly AI is being deployed and how slowly governance is being built widens with every system added. At some point, something goes wrong — and there is no foundation to fall back on.
risk.reputational: In any investigation, the first question is what the organisation did when it knew about a problem. If the answer is nothing, that is the finding. The absence of a plan is its own evidence.

remediation: Name someone as responsible for AI governance. Write it down. Give them 30 days to produce a plan — even a one-page document with milestones is enough to establish that you are taking this seriously.
Review every live AI system against the three-plane model. Governance, Decision, Verification. Work out which elements are missing across each one.
Start with the Decision Plane and Verification Plane. These close the most serious gaps and produce the audit records that regulators and insurers need to see.

dpia_mapping.processing_description: Multiple ungoverned AI deployments operating without remediation roadmap or corrective action following identified incidents
dpia_mapping.risk: Critical — pattern of inaction across multiple systems creates compounding regulatory exposure; each ungoverned deployment adds to systemic risk
dpia_mapping.mitigation: Written governance roadmap with named owner and milestones; architecture review; immediate implementation of Decision and Verification Planes
dpia_mapping.residual_risk: Medium — after roadmap produced, residual risk from implementation delays; requires milestone tracking and board-level accountability

gaps.pain_line: This is the position that looks worst in any investigation — not a single gap, but a pattern of gaps with no plan. That is the evidence regulators use to distinguish oversight from wilful non-compliance.
gaps.severity_plain: Creates the most serious compound exposure available. A pattern of unaddressed governance failures is harder to defend than any individual gap. This is what triggers supervisory intervention rather than a compliance notice.
gaps.what_happens_next: Designate a named individual responsible for AI governance and give them 30 days to produce a written plan — even a one-page document with milestones is enough to show the organisation is taking this seriously. These issues can be identified and prioritised through a structured CLEARANCE engagement.

exposure_logic.note: All structural gaps present simultaneously — remediation absence is catastrophic
Known incidents, no corrective action — knowing inaction

recurrence_logic.note: No corrective action documented — likelihood of continued unaddressed exposure is certain
Multiple high gaps with no roadmap — compounding exposure

gaps.title: No DPIA for AI employee monitoring activity
gaps.description: You are using AI tools to monitor employees and no Data Protection Impact Assessment has been done. UK GDPR requires a DPIA before systematic AI monitoring of employees begins — not after, not retrospectively. Before. You started the monitoring without one. Every piece of data collected since then has no lawful foundation.
evidence_signals: Ask for the DPIA completed before this monitoring tool was deployed. It does not exist
The monitoring tool went live before any privacy risk assessment was conducted
HR leadership is unaware that a DPIA is legally required before systematic employee monitoring begins
No ICO pre-consultation was conducted despite high residual risk from AI monitoring

risk.regulatory: Running AI monitoring without a DPIA is unlawful from the day the monitoring started. That is an ICO enforcement matter — and it applies regardless of whether any individual has been harmed.
risk.operational: Any monitoring data gathered without a DPIA is legally compromised. It cannot safely be used in a performance review, a disciplinary process or any employment decision. If challenged, it falls apart.
risk.reputational: An ICO investigation that reveals employee monitoring without a DPIA is an employment story as much as a data protection one. Tribunal claims and enforcement action can run simultaneously.

remediation: Stop using monitoring data in any employment decision until a DPIA has been completed for each monitoring tool.
Complete a DPIA. If it identifies high residual risk, consult the ICO before the monitoring resumes. Document the outcome.
Set up an annual DPIA review for all monitoring tools. Record it. Make sure the DPO owns it.

dpia_mapping.processing_description: Systematic AI-based monitoring of employees covering productivity, communications, location or behaviour without DPIA
dpia_mapping.risk: High — systematic monitoring of employees is explicitly listed by ICO as processing likely to result in high risk requiring mandatory DPIA
dpia_mapping.mitigation: Complete DPIA before monitoring commences; ICO pre-consultation where high residual risk identified; annual review
dpia_mapping.residual_risk: Low — after DPIA completed and mitigations applied, residual risk from scope creep in monitoring; requires annual review and change management process

gaps.pain_line: This becomes visible during an ICO investigation or a data breach response — when a DPIA is requested and it becomes clear you never completed one.
gaps.severity_plain: Creates direct ICO enforcement exposure. Operating AI monitoring without a DPIA is unlawful from the date the monitoring commenced — regardless of whether any harm has occurred. That is not a future risk. It is a current breach.
gaps.what_happens_next: Stop using monitoring data in any employment decision until a DPIA is completed. Complete a DPIA for each monitoring tool before monitoring resumes. These issues can be identified and prioritised through a focused review of your HR monitoring practices.

exposure_logic.note: Incidents involving monitoring data confirm DPIA absence is actively harmful

recurrence_logic.note: No audit trail for monitoring — ICO cannot be satisfied retrospectively

gaps.title: AI employee monitoring not disclosed to staff
gaps.description: You are monitoring employees using AI tools and no one told them before it started. Productivity is tracked. Communications are flagged. Attendance is analysed. Your employees do not know. Every piece of monitoring data you have collected is legally compromised — and cannot be used in any employment decision.
evidence_signals: Ask your employees whether AI tools are monitoring their productivity or communications. Most will say no — but the tools are running
No monitoring policy was communicated to employees before monitoring began
The employee privacy notice does not reference AI monitoring activity
No employee acknowledgement record exists confirming receipt of a monitoring disclosure

risk.regulatory: UK GDPR requires employees to be told about monitoring before it begins. Not in the small print of a contract signed three years ago — properly told, specifically, about what is being tracked and why. Monitoring without that disclosure is unlawful.
risk.operational: Monitoring data collected without proper disclosure cannot be used in a disciplinary or performance process. If an Employment Tribunal finds that monitoring was undisclosed, the data becomes inadmissible and the procedure fails.
risk.reputational: Covert AI surveillance of employees — discovered through a subject access request, a tribunal or a whistleblower — destroys trust. It is also exactly what the ICO and parliamentary committees have been scrutinising.

remediation: Before the next working day: write a monitoring disclosure and send it to every affected employee. One page. Plain English. What is tracked, why, and what it is used for.
Update the employee privacy notice to include the monitoring activity. Get confirmation that employees have received it.
Review each monitoring tool. Can you demonstrate that the business objective requires this level of monitoring? If not, you need to document why it is proportionate.

dpia_mapping.processing_description: AI monitoring of employees without transparency disclosure — employees unaware of surveillance activity
dpia_mapping.risk: High — processing personal data without transparency is unlawful under UK GDPR Art 5(1)(a); all monitoring data affected
dpia_mapping.mitigation: Monitoring policy disclosed before monitoring recommences; privacy notice updated; staff acknowledgement recorded
dpia_mapping.residual_risk: Low — after disclosure implemented, residual risk from policy not reaching all affected staff; requires distribution records

gaps.pain_line: This becomes visible when an employee submits a subject access request — and discovers they have been monitored by tools you never told them about.
gaps.severity_plain: Creates direct ICO exposure under UK GDPR Article 5(1)(a). Undisclosed monitoring is unlawful. All monitoring data collected without disclosure is tainted — it cannot be used in performance reviews, disciplinary processes or employment decisions.
gaps.what_happens_next: Before the next working day: draft a one-page monitoring disclosure and send it to all affected employees. Until you do, do not use monitoring data in any employment decision. These issues can be identified and prioritised through a focused review of your HR monitoring practices.

exposure_logic.note: Employees actively monitored without disclosure — transparency breach is confirmed

recurrence_logic.note: Monitoring is live — disclosure gap affects every monitored employee now

gaps.title: Automated performance scoring without appeal mechanism
gaps.description: You are using AI to score employees or candidates and no one can explain how. A manager cannot explain why the system scored someone low. The employee cannot challenge it. It affected pay, a promotion or a hiring decision — and you have no process for review.
evidence_signals: An employee has asked why their score was low. The honest answer is: the system produced it and there is no formal way to challenge it
Managers rely on AI scores without a process for explaining or reviewing them
No appeal mechanism exists for employees affected by AI-influenced assessments
The AI scoring tool has not been tested for bias across protected characteristics

risk.regulatory: DUAA 2025 requires a right to human review where AI produces decisions with significant effects — and pay and promotion qualify. The Equality Act applies where AI scoring produces different outcomes across protected groups. Without an appeal process, neither obligation can be met.
risk.operational: Without a documented appeal mechanism, the employer cannot show a fair procedure at Employment Tribunal. An employee whose pay or promotion was affected by an AI score they cannot challenge has a straightforward procedural claim.
risk.reputational: AI scoring without transparency or appeal is one of the clearest examples of algorithmic management in public debate right now. An organisation that cannot explain how it scored its people has no defensible position.

remediation: This week: write a process — one paragraph — that tells employees how to ask for a human review of an AI-influenced score. Send it to all managers. That is the minimum.
Have the AI scoring tool tested for bias across protected characteristics before the next review cycle. Document the results.
Add a transparency notice to the performance process explaining that AI contributes to assessments and how someone can ask for a review.

dpia_mapping.processing_description: AI automated performance scoring producing significant effects on employment decisions without appeal mechanism
dpia_mapping.risk: High — automated scoring affecting pay and promotion constitutes ADM with significant effects; absence of appeal mechanism fails Art 22C mandatory safeguards
dpia_mapping.mitigation: Human review mechanism implemented; bias testing completed; transparency notice provided to employees
dpia_mapping.residual_risk: Medium — after appeal mechanism implemented, residual risk from bias in underlying model; requires ongoing monitoring of outcomes across protected characteristics

gaps.pain_line: This becomes visible the moment an employee asks why their score was low — and the honest answer is: we don't know, and there is no way to challenge it.
gaps.severity_plain: Creates exposure under DUAA 2025 Article 22C and the Equality Act 2010. Without an appeal mechanism, the employer cannot discharge mandatory ADM safeguards. A discrimination claim arising from AI scoring cannot be defended.
gaps.what_happens_next: This week: create a one-paragraph process telling employees how to request a human review of an AI-influenced assessment. Send it to all managers. This is the minimum that makes the next challenge defensible. These issues can be identified and prioritised through a focused review of your HR AI processes.

exposure_logic.note: AI performance scoring with no override or appeal — individual impact is uncontested

recurrence_logic.note: No record of how scores were calculated — appeal is impossible

gaps.title: Disciplinary decision support without human adjudication record
gaps.description: You used AI output in a disciplinary process and the file does not show the human decision. It shows what the AI produced. What the decision-maker concluded — in their own words, independently — is not there. That file cannot be defended at Employment Tribunal.
evidence_signals: Pull a recent disciplinary file involving AI analysis. Find the paragraph showing the manager's independent reasoning. It is not there
Disciplinary documentation references AI output but contains no independent human reasoning
No procedure requires managers to document their reasoning separately from AI analysis
Appeal records do not show independent review of the AI contribution to the decision

risk.regulatory: The ACAS Code requires documented, reasoned decisions for any disciplinary outcome. The Employment Rights Act requires a fair procedure as well as a fair reason. A file that shows AI output but no independent human reasoning fails both.
risk.operational: At Employment Tribunal, the employer must produce the decision record. Where that record shows AI output without independent human reasoning, the tribunal will question whether a human made the decision at all.
risk.reputational: An employee dismissed with AI involvement and no documented human reasoning is one of the most damaging HR stories going. The combination of AI and absent human judgment is exactly what media and regulators focus on.

remediation: Update the disciplinary procedure to require managers to document their independent reasoning — separately from any AI output — before any outcome is communicated.
Train managers on what that means in practice. Not a summary of the AI. Their reasoning. In their words. Signed and dated.
Review any open disciplinary cases involving AI to check the record is complete before anything is communicated.

dpia_mapping.processing_description: AI-assisted disciplinary investigations with no sealed human adjudication record
dpia_mapping.risk: Medium — AI involvement in disciplinary decisions without records creates Employment Tribunal exposure and Equality Act risk
dpia_mapping.mitigation: Updated procedure requiring AI contribution documentation; human reasoning recorded contemporaneously; appeal process with independent reviewer
dpia_mapping.residual_risk: Low — after documentation requirements embedded, residual risk from inconsistent application; requires manager training and periodic audit

gaps.pain_line: This becomes visible at Employment Tribunal — when you are asked to produce the decision record and the file shows AI output but no independent human reasoning.
gaps.severity_plain: Creates direct Employment Tribunal exposure. Without a contemporaneous human decision record, the employer cannot satisfy the fair procedure requirement under Employment Rights Act 1996 s.98. That case is very difficult to defend.
gaps.what_happens_next: Update the disciplinary procedure to require explicit documentation of AI tool use and the decision-maker's independent reasoning — before any outcome is communicated. These issues can be identified and prioritised through a focused review of your HR disciplinary processes.

exposure_logic.note: Disciplinary decisions challenged — AI involvement without human record is indefensible

gaps.title: AI suitability assessment without individual compliance review
gaps.description: Your AI system is generating suitability assessments and client-facing outputs without individual compliance review for every decision. The FCA requires that suitability assessments reflect individual client circumstances and are subject to appropriate oversight. You cannot demonstrate that each automated assessment was reviewed before it reached the client.
evidence_signals: Ask for the compliance sign-off record for the last 10 suitability assessments sent to clients. They do not exist
A defined percentage of client letters are generated and dispatched without individual review
No sampling protocol defines the minimum review rate or escalation threshold

risk.regulatory: FCA Consumer Duty requires firms to evidence that clients receive outcomes that are in their interest. risk.operational: If the FCA requests a suitability file for a specific client on a specific date and you cannot reproduce how the score was calculated, you have no defensible position. That is not a future risk — it applies to every assessment already sent.
risk.reputational: A mis-sold investment product traced to an unreviewed AI assessment creates regulatory, legal and media exposure simultaneously. The firm's authorisation is the terminal risk.

remediation: Define and document a minimum individual review rate for all AI-generated suitability outputs. Any client below a defined portfolio threshold must still be subject to a periodic file review — not zero review.
Implement a sealed decision log for every suitability assessment: date, input data snapshot, score output, and review status. That log must be producible on FCA request within 24 hours.
Assign a named Senior Manager under SM&CR with documented accountability for AI-assisted suitability decisions. That accountability must be recorded in the Statements of Responsibilities.

Implement a client disclosure statement confirming AI involvement in suitability assessments: clients must be informed before a recommendation is made that AI has been used in the process, and must be told how to request a human review of their assessment. Retain disclosure records per client file. The FCA treats absence of disclosure as a Consumer Duty transparency failure independent of the suitability outcome.

gaps.title: No reproducible audit trail for AI-driven financial decisions
gaps.description: Your AI system is making or materially influencing financial decisions and there is no tamper-evident, immutable audit trail showing what data was used, what output was produced, and what action followed. The FCA can request this record. You cannot produce it. Every decision made without this record is individually indefensible on request.
evidence_signals: Ask for the complete decision record for a specific client decision made three months ago. It cannot be produced
Decision logs capture the output only — not the input data, model version, or the reasoning path
No write-once or tamper-evident logging mechanism exists for AI decision outputs
The firm cannot confirm which version of the AI model produced a specific historical decision

risk.regulatory: The FCA requires firms to maintain adequate records of their activities. An AI system producing client-facing outputs without a reproducible decision record fails that requirement. When the FCA asks — and they will ask — the absence of the record is the breach, independent of whether any harm occurred.
risk.operational: Without a reproducible audit trail, the firm cannot defend a complaint, respond to a Subject Access Request, or support an FCA information request within the required timeframe. Every day the system runs without logging is another day of undefended decisions accumulating.
risk.reputational: A firm that cannot show the FCA how a specific financial decision was made — even retrospectively — signals that governance is absent at a fundamental operational level.

regulatory_links: MiFID II / UK MiFIR — transaction and order record requirements
remediation: Implement a tamper-evident, immutable decision log for every AI output: input data snapshot, model version identifier, output value, timestamp, and the action triggered. The log must be write-protected — no post-hoc modification permitted. This is the minimum reproducible record.
Define the retention period for decision logs in line with FCA SYSC 9 requirements for the relevant instrument or activity. Document it. Apply it consistently.
Run a retrospective audit of decisions made in the last 12 months. Identify the period for which no reproducible record exists. Flag that period as an unaudited exposure in your governance register.

Implement a controlled model change process: no change to the AI model — version update, parameter adjustment, or retraining — without a documented change record naming the approver, the date, and the version identifier. Without this, your audit trail breaks at every model change and historical decisions cannot be attributed to a specific model state.

gaps.description: Your AI system is producing client-facing outputs — recommendations, assessments, or decisions — and there is no evidence that those outputs deliver good outcomes for clients. Consumer Duty requires firms to be able to demonstrate this. You cannot. The outputs are going out and there is no documented basis on which to assert that they are delivering good outcomes.

risk.regulatory: FCA Consumer Duty (PS22/9) requires firms to monitor and evidence that their products and services deliver good outcomes for retail customers. An AI-driven process with no outcome monitoring fails that requirement at the point of the next supervisory review — or the next annual board attestation.
risk.operational: Without outcome monitoring, the firm cannot identify whether its AI system is systematically producing poor recommendations for any client segment. By the time the problem surfaces — through complaints or FCA review — the scale of remediation required is materially larger.
risk.reputational: The FCA's Consumer Duty framework was designed to catch exactly this pattern — a firm deploying automated processes that look efficient but cannot demonstrate client benefit. Enforcement action under Consumer Duty carries public censure.

remediation: Define the client outcomes your AI system is intended to deliver. Document them. These become the baseline against which you monitor — without a defined outcome, you cannot evidence achievement of it.

Implement a minimum quarterly outcome review covering AI-generated recommendations: complaint rates, client retention, product appropriateness challenges, and any FCA feedback. That review must be documented and presented to the board.

Apply a vulnerability screening step to AI-generated outputs before dispatch — identify whether any client segment is receiving systematically different or potentially harmful outputs and document what action is taken.

gaps.title: No bias or fairness controls on AI-driven client decisions
gaps.description: Your AI system is producing recommendations or decisions that affect clients differently and there are no controls to detect or prevent systematic bias in those outputs. You have not assessed whether the system produces materially different outcomes for clients sharing a protected characteristic. The absence of a documented bias assessment is itself evidence of non-compliance when requested by the FCA. Additionally, clients have not been informed that AI is involved in the decisions affecting them — a disclosure obligation under Consumer Duty that the absence of a bias framework compounds.
evidence_signals: Ask for the bias assessment completed for the AI model before deployment. It does not exist
No demographic or protected characteristic analysis has been run against the AI system's output distribution
The model was not tested for differential outputs across age, gender or other protected characteristics before going live
No ongoing monitoring checks whether output distributions are shifting in ways that correlate with protected characteristics

risk.regulatory: The FCA expects firms to treat customers fairly and to identify and mitigate the risk of discriminatory outcomes from automated systems. The Equality Act 2010 applies to financial services. An AI system producing systematically different outcomes for clients sharing a protected characteristic — without detection — creates both FCA and Equality Act exposure simultaneously.
risk.operational: Algorithmic bias in a financial services context typically compounds over time — the longer the system runs without a bias assessment, the larger the cohort of clients who may have received systematically different treatment. Remediation at scale is operationally disruptive and expensive.
risk.reputational: An FCA or press investigation identifying that an AI system was making biased financial decisions — and that the firm had no controls to detect it — is categorically damaging. It cannot be defended as an oversight.

regulatory_links: Equality Act 2010 — ss.13, 19 (direct and indirect discrimination)
FCA FG22/5 — Final Non-Handbook Guidance on Consumer Duty
remediation: Commission a bias assessment of the AI model before the next deployment cycle — specifically testing for differential output distributions across age, gender, and other protected characteristics relevant to your client base. Document the outcome.

Implement ongoing output distribution monitoring: a quarterly statistical check on whether recommendation or decision outputs are shifting in ways that correlate with protected characteristics. Flag and investigate any statistically significant variance.

Add a fairness attestation to the model approval process for any AI system touching client-facing decisions: no model goes live without a documented bias assessment signed off by a named Senior Manager.

Implement a client disclosure statement for all AI-assisted financial decisions: clients must be informed, in plain English, that AI is used in the process affecting them, what it does, and how they can request a human review. Document the disclosure mechanism and retain records per matter. This is a Consumer Duty transparency requirement — the absence of disclosure is independently reviewable by the FCA.

gaps.title: AI-assisted claims or underwriting decision without consumer-facing explanation mechanism
gaps.description: Your AI system is influencing claims outcomes, underwriting decisions, or pricing determinations and there is no mechanism to explain those decisions to the affected policyholder in plain terms. The consumer cannot understand why a claim was declined, a premium was set, or coverage was restricted — and has no documented route to challenge it. This is not an audit trail gap (G15) — it is a consumer-facing transparency failure. FCA Consumer Duty requires firms to demonstrate that AI-assisted decisions produce good outcomes and that consumers can understand and contest them. EIOPA has separately identified explainability as a supervisory priority for insurance AI. The absence of an explanation mechanism is independently reviewable and cannot be defended as a resourcing constraint.
evidence_signals: Ask for the standard explanation issued to a policyholder when an AI system influences a claim decline. It does not exist or is a generic template with no decision-specific content
No process exists for a policyholder to request a human review of an AI-assisted underwriting or claims decision
The firm cannot produce a documented explanation chain linking the AI output to the decision communicated to the consumer
No disclosure is made to the consumer that AI was involved in the decision affecting them

risk.regulatory: FCA Consumer Duty (PS22/9) requires firms to demonstrate good outcomes for retail customers — an AI-assisted claims or underwriting decision that the consumer cannot understand or challenge is a documented Consumer Duty failure. EIOPA's February 2025 consultation on AI governance explicitly identifies explainability as a supervisory expectation for insurers. The EU AI Act classifies insurance underwriting AI as high-risk, mandating human oversight and transparency obligations from August 2026.
risk.operational: Without an explanation mechanism, every disputed claim or underwriting decision requires ad hoc reconstruction — an expensive, inconsistent, and legally exposed process. A single FOS complaint or FCA supervisory visit that reveals the absence of an explanation framework escalates from a process gap to a governance failure.
risk.reputational: An insurer that cannot explain to a policyholder why their claim was declined — and cannot demonstrate that AI was not the sole decision-maker — faces press and regulatory exposure that is disproportionate to the cost of implementing the control.

regulatory_links: FCA Consumer Duty (PS22/9) — good outcomes, consumer understanding

remediation: Define and document an explanation standard for all AI-assisted claims and underwriting decisions: for each decision type, specify what the consumer must be told — in plain English — about what AI assessed, what it concluded, and what the consumer can do next. Template the explanation, do not leave it to individual handlers.

Implement a documented human review pathway: any consumer who disputes an AI-assisted decision must have a named, accessible route to a human adjudicator who can override the AI output. Record every invocation and outcome.

Add consumer AI disclosure to all policy documentation and decision communications: the consumer must be informed that AI is used in the process affecting them before the decision is made, not after. This is a Consumer Duty transparency requirement independent of the explainability obligation.

Map each AI-assisted decision type to a DPIA: document the processing, the explanation standard, the human override mechanism, and the residual risk. This is the audit artefact that satisfies both FCA and EIOPA supervisory requests.

fs_modifiers.description: Friction Signal modifiers — signals that boost severity or likelihood of any fired gap when present. Applied after gap evaluation, before priority calculation.
fs_modifiers.application_rule: For each fired gap: check each modifier. If if_signal is true and gap_id matches applies_to (or applies_to=['all']), add severity_boost to gap severity_score and likelihood_boost to gap likelihood_score before computing priority.

no_smcr_ai_owner.reason: Absence of named SM&CR owner elevates likelihood across all gaps — no individual is accountable for oversight or remediation, increasing probability that gaps persist and compound

has_incidents.reason: Known incidents confirm the gap is not theoretical — severity elevated for boundary, audit and remediation gaps where incident evidence is most damaging

no_corrective_action.reason: Known gap with documented inaction — knowing inaction is the most severe governance posture. Both severity and likelihood elevated for remediation and audit trail gaps where inaction narrative is most consequential

no_outcome_monitoring.reason: Complete absence of Consumer Duty outcome monitoring elevates severity — board attestation failure is a current, documented compliance absence rather than a process gap

no_bias_assessment.reason: Absence of any documented bias assessment is itself evidence of non-compliance on FCA request — elevates severity beyond the gap being merely unaddressed

all_gaps_present.reason: All structural gaps simultaneously present — compounding exposure elevates both severity and likelihood for the remediation gap to maximum

steps.name: Base score resolution

steps.name: FS modifier application
steps.logic: For each modifier in fs_modifiers: if if_signal is true AND gap_id is in applies_to (or applies_to=['all']), add severity_boost and likelihood_boost to scores. Cap at 5.
